author: A Robot
objectives: Students will determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Students will predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number, identifying the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.
Students will distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Students will explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
Students will apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules and compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

modules.description: Students learn the fundamental principle of VSEPR theory—that electron pairs repel each other and arrange to minimize repulsion—and are introduced to the concept of electron domains and steric number.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Understand the basic principle of VSEPR theory and how electron pair repulsion drives molecular geometry.
Define electron domains and steric number, and learn to count both from Lewis structures.

components.text: VSEPR Theory: How Electron Pairs Shape Molecules

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction text and central atom with two electron domains displayed to establish the basic concept of electron pair repulsion and molecular geometry.
clips.narration: Welcome to VSEPR theory! VSEPR stands for Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion. The central idea is elegant: electron pairs—whether they form bonds or exist as lone pairs—repel each other. Atoms arrange their electron domains in three-dimensional space to minimize this repulsion. This simple principle explains the shapes of nearly all covalent molecules.

components.text: Steric Number: Count All Electron Domains

clips.changeMeaning: Text label added to show definition of steric number and clarify what counts as an electron domain.
clips.narration: To predict molecular geometry, we must first count the steric number of the central atom. The steric number is the total number of electron domains attached to the central atom. An electron domain is a region of electron density—this includes bonding pairs and lone pairs. Count each bond (single, double, or triple) as one domain, and count each lone pair as one domain.

modules.description: Students explore the five fundamental electron-domain geometries that result from different steric numbers (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, octahedral) and observe how 3D objects arrange themselves to minimize repulsion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify and visualize the five electron-domain geometries corresponding to steric numbers 2 through 6.
Understand that electron domains spread out in three-dimensional space and explain the predicted bond angles for each geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: Five electron-domain geometry models displayed side-by-side with steric number labels, showing the relationship between steric number and 3D arrangement of electron domains.
clips.narration: As electron domains repel each other, they arrange in space to maximize the distance between them. The resulting geometry depends on the steric number—the total count of electron domains. With two domains, they point in opposite directions, giving a linear geometry with a 180° angle. With three domains, they spread into a plane with 120° angles, forming a trigonal planar geometry. Four domains arrange into a tetrahedral shape with 109.5° angles.

clips.changeMeaning: Continued explanation of trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral geometries, reinforcing how electron domains spread to minimize repulsion.
clips.narration: Five domains arrange into a trigonal bipyramidal geometry: three domains in an equatorial plane at 120° angles, and two domains pointing axially (above and below) at 90° angles to the equator. Finally, with six domains, all pointing toward the corners of an octahedron, every domain is 90° away from its nearest neighbors. These five electron-domain geometries are the foundation of VSEPR predictions.

modules.description: Students learn to distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry by observing how lone pairs modify the shape, and explore why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, causing bond-angle compressions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry, recognizing that lone pairs occupy space but atoms are not drawn.
Predict molecular geometry for molecules with lone pairs by removing the lone-pair positions from the electron-domain geometry.
Explain qualitatively why lone pair–bonding pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair–bonding pair repulsion, leading to bond-angle deviations.

clips.changeMeaning: Three molecular models displayed—methane, ammonia, and water—showing progressively more lone pairs and the resulting reduction in bond angles.
clips.narration: Here's a crucial distinction: electron-domain geometry describes the arrangement of all electron domains around the central atom. But molecular geometry describes only the positions of atoms—we don't include the lone pairs when naming the shape. Consider methane, CH4. Carbon has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so its electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry are both tetrahedral with perfect 109.5° angles.

clips.changeMeaning: Explanation of how lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, causing bond-angle deviations from idealized tetrahedral values.
clips.narration: Now compare ammonia, NH3. Nitrogen has four electron domains: three bonding pairs and one lone pair. The electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral. But the molecular geometry describes only the three hydrogen atoms, so we call it trigonal pyramidal. Notice that ammonia's bond angles compress slightly to about 107° from the ideal 109.5°. This happens because a lone pair occupies more angular space than a bonding pair. The lone pair's electron density is concentrated on just the central atom, creating stronger repulsion with neighboring bonding pairs. Water, H2O, takes this further: two lone pairs and two bonding pairs give a tetrahedral electron-domain geometry that becomes bent molecular geometry, with a measured bond angle of only 104.5°.

modules.description: Students apply VSEPR theory to predict the geometries of specific molecules—water, ammonia, methane, phosphorus pentafluoride, sulfur hexafluoride, and xenon tetrafluoride—and compare predictions to experimental structures.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Apply the VSEPR prediction process (count steric number, identify electron-domain geometry, account for lone pairs) to diverse molecules.
Match predicted molecular geometries from VSEPR theory to experimentally determined structures.
Recognize limitations of VSEPR (bond-angle fine-tuning) while acknowledging its remarkable predictive power for main-group molecules.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduction to the structured VSEPR prediction process, setting up the analysis of real molecules displayed.
clips.narration: Now we apply VSEPR systematically. The process is: first, draw the Lewis structure and identify the central atom. Second, count all electron domains around the central atom—bonding pairs and lone pairs. Third, identify the electron-domain geometry for that steric number. Fourth, identify which domains are lone pairs and remove them to get the molecular geometry. Let's test this on real molecules.

clips.changeMeaning: Detailed analysis of six key molecules, demonstrating the application of VSEPR predictions to diverse real-world structures.
clips.narration: Water, H2O: steric number 4 (two bonds, two lone pairs), electron-domain geometry tetrahedral, molecular geometry bent with a 104.5° angle. Ammonia, NH3: steric number 4 (three bonds, one lone pair), electron-domain geometry tetrahedral, molecular geometry trigonal pyramidal with about 107° angles. Methane, CH4: steric number 4 (four bonds, no lone pairs), both geometries are tetrahedral with 109.5° angles. Phosphorus pentafluoride, PF5: steric number 5 (five bonds, no lone pairs), trigonal bipyramidal with equatorial angles of 120° and axial angles of 90°. Sulfur hexafluoride, SF6: steric number 6 (six bonds, no lone pairs), octahedral with all angles 90°. Xenon tetrafluoride, XeF4: steric number 6 (four bonds, two lone pairs arranged axially), electron-domain geometry octahedral, but molecular geometry square planar because the two lone pairs occupy the axial positions.
